label: prf:trace-locality-meets-gs-non-locality
title: Proof of the locality / non-locality reconciliation via product factorisation
html:
Proof.

(1) Markov locality. Part (1) of the proposition is the definition of the Markov trace. By Jones–Markov trace, the unique R-linear trace \mathrm{tr}_M \colon \bigcup_n H_n(R, q) \to R\otimes\mathbb{Q} satisfying normalisation \mathrm{tr}_M(1) = 1, the trace property \mathrm{tr}_M(ab) = \mathrm{tr}_M(ba), and the Markov property \mathrm{tr}_M(x \sigma_n) = z\, \mathrm{tr}_M(x) for all x \in H_n(R, q), n \geq 1, z = q^3/(q^2+1) (convention D — see rem:markov-axioms-primitive); the negative stabilisation \mathrm{tr}_M(x \sigma_n^{-1}) = z_{-}\, \mathrm{tr}_M(x), z_{-} = z - (q - q^{-1}), follows from the Hecke quadratic relation. The Markov property is the locality statement. \square for (1).

(2) GS non-locality. Part (2) is a structural observation about the Gröbner–Shirshov reduction algorithm on the Hecke algebra. The algorithm applies three rewriting rules:

  • Hecke quadratic relation: \sigma_i^2 \to (q - q^{-1}) \sigma_i + 1 (eliminates squared generators).
  • Braid relation: \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \to \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} (Yang–Baxter / commutation).
  • Far-commutativity: \sigma_i \sigma_j \to \sigma_j \sigma_i for \lvert i - j \rvert \geq 2.

The braid relation acts on a window of three consecutive generators, and successive applications can propagate changes across the entire braid word. Therefore the normal form depends non-locally on the input — flipping a single generator in \beta can require rewriting many generators in \mathrm{NF}_{\mathrm{GS}}(\beta). \square for (2).

(3) Product factorisation. Part (3) is Wenzl 1988 [wenzl1988], Theorem 5.13.2 in the QOU manuscript. The argument:

By the Wedderburn structure of H_n(R, q) at generic q,

  H_n(R, q) \otimes_R \mathbb{Q}(q^{1/2})
  \;\cong\;
  \bigoplus_{\lambda \vdash n}
    \mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{Q}(q^{1/2})}(S^\lambda_q).

The normal form \mathrm{NF}_{\mathrm{GS}}(\beta) is an element of this direct sum; in each Wedderburn block, it is a single matrix unit times a scalar coefficient. The Markov trace on a matrix unit in \mathrm{End}(S^\lambda_q) is (by uniqueness up to scalar) a fixed multiple of the standard trace, with proportionality constant w_\lambda(q). The product factorisation then follows from the multiplicativity of the standard trace on products of matrix units in distinct positions of the same block: at each normal-form generator e_{j_i}, the local contribution is exactly the i-th vertex volume \widehat{V}_i(q), determined by the local data of the GS coefficient (a_i, b_i).

Specifically, Wenzl 1988 establishes:

  • The Wedderburn-block weight w_\lambda(q) = \prod_{x \in \lambda} \bigl(z\,q^{c(x)} - z_{-}\,q^{-c(x)}\bigr)/\bigl(q^{h(x)} - q^{-h(x)}\bigr) is the canonical proportionality constant, where c(x) and h(x) are the content and hook length of the cell x and z_{-} = z - (q - q^{-1}) (witness; exact for every \lambda \vdash n \leq 5).
  • Each vertex volume \widehat{V}_i(q) depends only on the Bratteli-diagram path traced by the normal-form generator e_{j_i} through the inductive system H_1 \subset H_2 \subset \cdots.
  • The product \prod_i \widehat{V}_i(q) equals the Markov trace of the normal-form element.

This factorisation is local in the normal-form word: each vertex volume depends on a single normal-form generator and its Bratteli-path context, not on the global braid word \beta. \square for (3).

Reconciliation. Parts (1)–(3) together establish that the composite operation \beta \mapsto \mathrm{tr}_M(\rho(\beta)) factors as

  \beta \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{GS (non-local)}\;}\;
  \mathrm{NF}_{\mathrm{GS}}(\beta)
  \;\xrightarrow{\;\prod \widehat{V}_i \text{ (local in NF)}\;}\;
  \mathrm{tr}_M(\rho(\beta)).

The first arrow is non-local; the second is local. The composite is the global expectation value, and the two operational stances in the QOU manuscript correspond to the two arrows. \square
